inputs.question: Expected data volume and request rate
inputs.answer: No traffic, volume or deployment sizing in the repository

completeness.repository_coverage: All source under src/Conduit (handlers, domain, infrastructure, startup) read; tests and build scripts skimmed only.

unknowns.subject: Query plans and real table sizes
unknowns.what_would_resolve_it: EXPLAIN output and row counts from a representative database

unknowns.subject: Provider-generated SQL shape for the list query
unknowns.what_would_resolve_it: Enable EF command logging in a test and capture the SQL

known: SQLite is the default provider (src/Conduit/Program.cs); SQL Server optional
Schema created by EnsureCreated; no HasIndex in the model
No caching layer in the code
assumed: Tables grow to many thousands of rows (affects PERF-001, PERF-004, PERF-005)

decision_changing_questions.question: What table sizes and request concurrency are expected, and which database provider is deployed?
decision_changing_questions.what_it_would_change: Confidence and severity of PERF-001, PERF-003, PERF-005

root_causes.description: No secondary indexes on filtered and sorted columns
Article list unbounded and over-fetching with blocking count
Whole comment collection materialized for single-row operations
Follow relationships loaded in full for membership tests
Transaction on every request incl. reads, synchronous
Per-item round trips on article create

findings.problem: The model declares no secondary indexes. Article.Slug, Person.Username and Person.Email, which almost every request filters on, and Article.CreatedAt, the list sort key, are unindexed; the schema comes from EnsureCreated.
findings.performance_principle: Lookups by a selective key must be served by an index so cost is O(log n), not a scan of the whole table.

evidence.statement: OnModelCreating configures only composite keys and FKs; a search for HasIndex/[Index] across src finds none.
Slug lookups: Articles Details, Comments List/Create/Delete, Favorites, Edit all filter x.Slug == slug.
Username lookup on every authenticated write and in feed/profile paths; Email lookup in Login and Create.
List orders by CreatedAt then ArticleId with Skip/Take; no index on CreatedAt.
Schema created with EnsureCreated at startup; no migrations directory exists.

findings.conditions: Matters once Articles/Persons tables hold many thousands of rows (assumed; no data volume in the repo). Negligible on the small demo dataset.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for HasIndex, [Index], IndexAttribute, migrations and raw SQL DDL; none found. Providers create indexes only for FKs, not these columns (provider behavior, not verified by EXPLAIN).
Runtime query plans are not available, so scan behavior is inferred from the model alone.

findings.recommendation: Add unique indexes on Article.Slug, Person.Username, Person.Email and an index on Article.CreatedAt (or (CreatedAt, ArticleId)) via HasIndex; adopt migrations so the schema is versioned. Unique indexes also enforce the uniqueness the handlers check by query.
findings.trade_offs: Extra write cost and storage per insert; existing databases need a migration and a duplicate check before a unique index is created.

validation.metric: Query plan for WHERE Slug = @p and for ORDER BY CreatedAt DESC LIMIT 20 on a representative data volume
validation.expectation: Plan changes from table SCAN to index SEARCH; latency of slug-keyed endpoints stops growing with row count.
validation.falsifier: Plans already show index seeks, or p95 is flat as rows grow.
validation.guard: Integration test asserting the model contains the expected indexes.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: RealWorld is a demo app; if production tables stay small, scans are cheap and SQLite may be fast enough.

alternatives.option: Add HasIndex on the filtered columns
alternatives.why: Removes scans at the cause and also gives integrity.

findings.problem: The article list endpoint accepts an unbounded limit and offset, eager-loads Author, all ArticleFavorites and all ArticleTags for each row through joins, loads the full Body only to null it, and runs a second query for the total count.
findings.performance_principle: Work and response size per request must be bounded by a server-enforced cap, and fetch only the data the response uses.

evidence.statement: limit is taken as message.Limit ?? 20 with no upper bound; offset unvalidated.
GetAllData includes Author, ArticleFavorites and ArticleTags; rows multiply as favorites x tags per article in a single join (or split-query round trips).
Body is loaded then set to null per article in a loop.
Favorites are loaded as full rows only to derive Favorited and FavoritesCount.

findings.conditions: Any client can request a very large limit; this is the main browse endpoint. Cost also grows with favorites and tags per article and with deep offsets (assumed popular content).

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for a limit clamp, validator or paging options; none found for List.Query.
Default of 20 bounds the common case.

findings.recommendation: Clamp limit (for example to a documented maximum) and reject negative offsets; project to a DTO that selects only needed columns (no Body), with favorites as COUNT/EXISTS subqueries and tags as a bounded list; consider keyset pagination.
findings.trade_offs: Changing response shaping needs care to keep the API output identical; a cap is a visible behavior change for clients asking above it.

validation.metric: Rows and bytes returned per GET /articles; SQL statements per request at limit=20 and a very large limit
validation.expectation: Row count per page equals page size; response size no longer scales with an unbounded limit.
validation.falsifier: Logged SQL shows no duplicated rows and large limits are already rejected.
validation.guard: Test that limit above the cap is clamped.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Default page size is 20, and the cartesian factor is small if articles have few tags and favorites.

alternatives.why: Fewer duplicated rows but more round trips and still loads unused data.

findings.problem: The total count is computed with the synchronous queryable.Count() inside an async handler, blocking a thread-pool thread for the duration of a separate database query.
findings.performance_principle: Do not block threads on I/O in an async request path; blocked threads reduce capacity for all requests.

evidence.statement: ArticlesCount = queryable.Count() in the return statement of an async method.
The count query repeats the Tag/Author/Favorited/feed filters over the same data.

findings.conditions: Concurrent list requests on a database with non-trivial latency (SQL Server) or a large unindexed table; thread-pool starvation needs concurrency well above core count (assumed).

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for CountAsync usage; none in the handler.
The default SQLite provider is in-process and its calls are largely synchronous anyway, lowering impact there.

findings.recommendation: Use await queryable.CountAsync(cancellationToken); consider whether an exact total is needed on every page.

validation.metric: Thread-pool queue length and p95 of GET /articles under concurrent load
validation.falsifier: No change in thread-pool metrics at the target concurrency.
validation.guard: Analyzer rule flagging sync EF calls in async methods.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: With in-process SQLite the async calls are effectively synchronous and the difference is small.

findings.problem: Comment list, create and delete load every comment on the article (Include(Comments)); list also includes each comment's Author; there is no paging. Create loads all comments merely to add one.
findings.performance_principle: Do not materialize an unbounded collection when the operation needs one row or a page.

evidence.statement: Create includes x.Comments to add one comment.
List includes Comments.ThenInclude(Author) and returns the whole collection.
Delete includes Comments to remove one.

findings.conditions: Articles that accumulate many comments (assumed; no data volume known); hot articles concentrate the cost.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for paging in Comments handlers and controller; none. The RealWorld spec returns all comments, which limits how far paging can go.

findings.recommendation: In Create and Delete, query only the article id and the target comment instead of including the collection; for List, project to a DTO and add an optional cap or paging.
findings.trade_offs: Paging changes the contract beyond the spec; keep any cap generous.

validation.metric: Rows loaded by POST /articles/{slug}/comments for an article with many comments
validation.expectation: Constant row count independent of existing comments.
validation.falsifier: SQL log shows a single-row path already.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: The spec expects the full comment list, and typical comment counts per article are small.

alternatives.why: Invalidation on each write for little gain.

findings.problem: To answer a single yes/no (is this person followed), the code loads the current user's Following and Followers collections; the feed and list paths load all followed ids into memory and use List.Contains per author.
findings.performance_principle: Test membership with a targeted keyed query instead of loading the full relationship set.

evidence.statement: Persons.Include(Following).Include(Followers) then Followers.Any(x => x.TargetId == person.PersonId). Following holds the people who follow the current user.
Feed loads currentUser with Include(Followers) and filters with currentUser.Followers.Select(...).Contains(...).
List loads all followed ids into a list, then followedIds.Contains per article author.

findings.conditions: Authenticated users with large follower or following sets (assumed); profile reads and follow/unfollow all use ReadProfile.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for count or paging limits on follows; none.

findings.recommendation: Replace with AnyAsync on FollowedPeople keyed by (ObserverId, TargetId); for list decoration, query only the follow ids for the authors on the page (TargetId in page author ids).
findings.trade_offs: Extra small queries instead of one include; the primary key already supports the lookup.

validation.metric: Rows loaded by GET /profiles/{username} for a user with many followers
validation.falsifier: SQL log shows no collection load.

findings.why_this_might_not_matter: Most users follow few accounts; Following (who follows me) is only expensive for very popular accounts.

findings.problem: Serilog is configured at Verbose minimum level with a synchronous console sink and no per-namespace overrides, so framework and EF Core command logging is written to the console on every request.
findings.performance_principle: Per-request instrumentation overhead must be proportionate; log volume on hot paths should be controlled by level.

evidence.statement: MinimumLevel.Verbose() with only a Console sink, commented as just for local debug.

findings.conditions: Production deployment using this code as-is (the Dockerfile runs it unchanged) at moderate or higher request rates.

counter_evidence.statement: No appsettings or environment override found for log level; no config file in src/Conduit.
Actual log volume and console throughput are unmeasured.

findings.recommendation: Make the level configurable (Information or Warning by default with Microsoft.* overrides) and read it from configuration.

validation.metric: Log lines per request and p95 latency with level Verbose versus Warning
validation.expectation: Fewer lines and lower per-request overhead.

findings.problem: Every mediator request, including read-only queries, opens a ReadCommitted transaction using synchronous BeginTransaction/Commit, adding round trips and holding the connection for the whole handler.
findings.performance_principle: Per-request fixed overhead should be limited to work the request needs; do not use blocking calls on async paths.

evidence.statement: BeginTransaction and CommitTransaction wrap next() for all requests; calls are synchronous.
BeginTransaction skips only the in-memory provider.

findings.conditions: High read rates on SQL Server, where each transaction adds begin/commit round trips; on SQLite the cost is small but a write transaction serializes writers.

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for opt-outs for queries (marker interface); none.

findings.recommendation: Apply the transaction behavior only to commands, and use BeginTransactionAsync/CommitAsync.
findings.trade_offs: Handlers that rely on read consistency across several queries would lose the snapshot unless they opt in.

findings.problem: Article creation does a lookup plus SaveChanges per new tag, and probes slug uniqueness with a query loop that issues one query per collision; the slug query is unindexed.
findings.performance_principle: Batch writes and avoid per-item round trips inside a request.

evidence.statement: Per-tag FindAsync and immediate SaveChangesAsync inside foreach.
AnyAsync slug loop in Create and Edit.

findings.conditions: Articles created with many tags or repeated identical titles (assumed uncommon).

counter_evidence.statement: Tag count per article is user-supplied and unbounded in the model, but typical use is a few tags.

findings.recommendation: Resolve all tags with one query and save once; generate unique slugs with a suffix or rely on a unique index and retry.
findings.trade_offs: Concurrent creation of the same tag needs handling of unique-violation retries.

validation.metric: SQL statements per POST /articles with 10 tags

findings.problem: The tags endpoint reads the entire Tags table on every call with no paging or caching.
findings.performance_principle: Unbounded reads of a growing set should be bounded or served from a reusable result.

evidence.statement: Tags.OrderBy(TagId).ToListAsync() with no limit.

findings.conditions: Large tag vocabulary (every distinct user-supplied tag is stored) and a client that calls this on every page load (assumed).

counter_evidence.statement: Searched for caching and limits; none.

findings.recommendation: Return top-N tags by usage or add a short-lived cache only after measuring tag count and call rate.
findings.trade_offs: Spec expects all tags; limiting changes output.

validation.metric: Row count of Tags and calls/min to GET /tags
validation.expectation: Decision input for capping or caching.

considered_not_reported.observation: Password hashing uses a single keyed HMAC-SHA512 pass, which is cheap per login (no CPU amplification).
considered_not_reported.why_discarded: Not a performance problem; the weakness is a security matter reported as SEC-001.
considered_not_reported.revisit_when: If the hash is replaced by a deliberately slow KDF, move it off the request thread or bound login concurrency.

adjacent_findings.problem: Passwords are hashed with a single HMAC-SHA512 pass using a hard-coded key and a GUID salt, and the JWT signing key, issuer and audience are hard-coded in source. Hash comparison uses SequenceEqual (not constant time).

evidence.statement: HMACSHA512 keyed with a literal string.
Signing key literal in AddJwt.

adjacent_findings.recommendation: Use a slow password KDF (ASP.NET Core PasswordHasher, Argon2 or PBKDF2 with iterations) and load signing keys from secret configuration.
adjacent_findings.assessed_properly_by: A dedicated security review and dependency/secret scan
